cards.title: Introduction to Variables
cards.content:
A variable is a container that holds data during the execution of a Java program. Every variable is assigned a data type, which designates the method and limits of its data storage.

To use a variable, you must first declare it and then initialize it:

int age; // Declaration
age = 25; // Initialization

int score = 100; // Declaration and Initialization in one line

cards.title: Java Data Types Overview
cards.content:
Java is a strongly-typed language, meaning all variables must be declared with a specific type before they can be used. Java data types are divided into two main categories:

  • Primitive Types: Predefined by the language (e.g., int, double, boolean, char). They store raw values directly in memory.
  • Reference Types: Created by the programmer (except for String, which is built-in). They store references (memory addresses) to objects.

cards.title: Numeric Data Types
cards.content:
Java provides several primitive types for storing numbers, depending on their size and precision requirements:

  • Integer Types: byte (8-bit), short (16-bit), int (32-bit), and long (64-bit).
  • Floating-Point Types: float (32-bit single-precision) and double (64-bit double-precision).
long population = 8000000000L; // Note the 'L' suffix
float temperature = 36.6f;     // Note the 'f' suffix
double price = 19.99;

cards.title: Char and Boolean Types
cards.content:
Besides numbers, Java has types to manage characters and logical states:

  • char: Represents a single 16-bit Unicode character. It must be enclosed in single quotes.
  • boolean: Represents a logical state and can only hold the values true or false.
char grade = 'A';
boolean isJavaFun = true;

cards.title: Variable Naming Rules & Conventions
cards.content:
When naming variables in Java, you must adhere to official rules and should follow community conventions:

  • Rules (Compiler enforced): Must start with a letter, $, or _. Cannot contain spaces or special characters. Cannot be a Java reserved keyword (e.g., class, void).
  • Conventions: Use camelCase (e.g., userAge, totalPrice). Names should be descriptive and meaningful.

cards.title: Scope of Variables
cards.content:
The scope of a variable determines where it can be accessed within your program:

  • Local Variables: Declared inside a method, constructor, or block. Visible only within that block.
  • Instance Variables (Fields): Declared inside a class but outside any method. Unique to each class instance.
  • Static Variables: Declared with the static keyword inside a class. Shared across all instances of that class.

options.text: Local variables can be accessed anywhere in the class.
Instance variables require an object instance to be accessed.
Static variables cannot be accessed by non-static methods.
Local variables must have the static modifier.

cards.title: Final Variables (Constants)
cards.content:
To prevent a variable's value from being reassigned after initialization, use the final keyword. This turns the variable into a constant.

final double PI = 3.14159;
// PI = 3.14; // This line would cause a compile-time error

By convention, final variable names are written in ALL_CAPS with underscores separating words.

cards.title: Local Variable Type Inference (var)
cards.content:
Starting in Java 10, you can use the var keyword for local variable type inference. The compiler automatically determines the type based on the assigned value.

var message = "Hello, World!"; // Compiler infers String
var count = 10;                // Compiler infers int

Note: var can only be used for local variables inside methods and must be initialized immediately during declaration.

cards.title: Variables Summary & Best Practices
cards.content:
Great job! Here is a recap of best practices for working with variables in Java:

  • Always choose the smallest data type appropriate for your numeric values to save memory.
  • Initialize variables as close as possible to their first use.
  • Use final by default unless a variable needs to change over time.
  • Follow camelCase conventions for readability across engineering teams.
